blocks.text: **Tumour lysis syndrome (TLS)** is an oncological emergency. A large mass of tumour cells is destroyed abruptly, usually by the **first course of anticancer treatment**, and the cells empty their contents into the bloodstream. The result is a cluster of metabolic disturbances that can injure the kidneys and the heart.

blocks.title: The TLS tetrad: three highs, one low
rows: Mainly intracellular ion, freed when cells burst
Mainly intracellular ion, freed when cells burst
Breakdown of released nucleic acids and purines
Secondary: bound and sequestered by the excess phosphate

blocks.text: Mnemonic **PUKE Calcium**: **P**hosphate, **U**rate and **K**+ are **E**levated, and **Calcium** is the only value that falls.
TLS belongs on the list of **chemotherapy complications**, alongside infection from immunosuppression, neurotoxicity, cardiotoxicity, infertility and second cancers.

TLS needs a tumour that is **bulky, fast-growing and chemosensitive**, so that treatment kills many cells at once. The classic culprits are **high-grade lymphomas (especially Burkitt)**, the **acute leukaemias** (ALL, AML, CML in blast crisis) and **germ cell tumours**.

blocks.title: Who is at high risk?
rows: Bulky disease; a high pre-treatment **LDH** reflects bulk

blocks.title: Triggers and timing
items: Typically a **first-dose / first-cycle** effect, especially in lymphoproliferative and other haematological cancers.
Even **corticosteroids alone** can provoke it, because they too can cause rapid death of malignant cells.
**Venetoclax** is specifically linked to TLS when it is started and needs close surveillance.
It can occur **spontaneously**, before any treatment, especially in leukaemia (rare).
In acute leukaemia, TLS sits beside leukostasis and DIC as a disease complication and is a recognised cause of acute kidney failure.

blocks.text: **Burkitt lymphoma** is the highest-risk scenario: the patient must be metabolically stable before therapy, everyone gets TLS prophylaxis (rasburicase if available), and potassium and phosphate are checked very often for **at least 72 hours**.

Solid tumours: Pocket Medicine calls TLS **very rare** with solid tumours, but Davidson includes bulky, chemosensitive **germ cell tumours**, and Step-Up adds any solid cancer with a very high tumour burden. Follow Davidson: think of TLS whenever a bulky, chemosensitive tumour is first treated.

When many cells die within a short time, their contents flood the extracellular fluid. **Potassium and phosphate** are mostly intracellular, so their plasma levels jump. **Nucleic acids and purines** are broken down to **uric acid**. The surplus phosphate then **binds calcium**, so hypocalcaemia follows.

blocks.title: Mechanism of each abnormality
items: **Hyperkalaemia**: K+ shifts from cells into plasma, the same mechanism as in rhabdomyolysis and severe haemolysis.
**Hyperphosphataemia**: phosphate moves from cells into plasma. It is made worse by phosphate-containing preparations or unwarranted vitamin D.
**Hyperuricaemia**: increased purine turnover. Serum urate can climb to **4–5 times** the upper limit of normal.
**Hypocalcaemia**: secondary to the high phosphate, which sequesters calcium.

blocks.text: **How the kidneys fail:** the large filtered urate load **crystallises in the tubules and interstitium**, giving an obstructive crystal uropathy (_hyperuricaemic_ or _urate nephropathy_). High phosphate adds **calcium phosphate deposits** in the tubules. The result is acute kidney injury.

blocks.title: Clinical features
rows: Perioral paraesthesia, cramps, tetany (Trousseau and Chvostek signs), seizures, prolonged QT

blocks.text: **Hyperkalaemia is the main danger** in TLS: it is the abnormality that kills quickly through arrhythmia.
Severe hyperuricaemia during chemotherapy **seldom causes gout**. Its real risk is **acute kidney injury**.

blocks.title: Before treatment: assess the risk
items: Assess TLS risk and start prevention **before induction chemotherapy** for acute leukaemia.
**LDH** correlates with tumour bulk and flags higher risk. It is also part of lymphoma staging.
**Baseline serum uric acid**, particularly in lymphomas that carry a TLS risk.
Routine biochemistry (renal function, electrolytes) for organ damage and evidence of early lysis.

blocks.title: After treatment starts: monitor closely
items: Check **potassium, phosphate, calcium, uric acid and creatinine** regularly for **48–72 hours** in at-risk patients.
A **rising potassium** may be the earliest biochemical sign.
In Burkitt lymphoma, keep monitoring potassium and phosphate very frequently for **at least 72 hours**.

blocks.title: ECG clues
rows: Tall peaked T waves, flattened or absent P waves, broad QRS. Record an ECG for any K+ above 6 mmol/L

blocks.title: If AKI develops: is it urate nephropathy?
items: **Urine microscopy** for uric acid crystals plus a **serum urate**.
A **urine uric acid : urine creatinine ratio above 1** supports acute uric acid nephropathy.

blocks.text: After **rasburicase**, the measured urate may be **undetectable**. That is the drug working, not proof that TLS is over. Keep watching potassium, phosphate, calcium and renal function.

**Hydration is the cornerstone** of both prevention and treatment. IV fluid dilutes the extracellular fluid, which eases the electrolyte disturbance, and expands circulating volume, which improves glomerular filtration and lets the kidney excrete potassium. In **high-risk patients start it 24 hours before treatment** and keep urine output high throughout. Diuretics are often added to keep the urine flowing. Kumar & Clark Essentials quotes about **4–5 L/day IV**. Urine output targets vary between manuals (about 80–100 mL/h, or at least 100 mL/m²/h).

blocks.title: Urate-lowering drugs
rows: Xanthine oxidase inhibitor: **stops new uric acid forming**
Recombinant urate oxidase: **converts existing uric acid to soluble allantoin**
Prophylaxis in lower-risk patients, with IV fluids
Prophylaxis in high-risk patients (e.g. Burkitt, high baseline urate) and treatment of established TLS
Blocks new urate formation; does not remove urate already present
Breaks down urate already present; level may become undetectable

blocks.title: Treating each abnormality
items: **Hyperkalaemia** (the immediate threat): treat aggressively. IV **calcium gluconate** stabilises the myocardium and **insulin with dextrose** shifts K+ into cells. K+ of 6.5 mmol/L or more needs urgent treatment whatever the ECG shows.
**Hyperphosphataemia**: IV normal saline promotes phosphate excretion, and **phosphate binders** can be given.
**Hypocalcaemia**: give calcium **only if symptomatic** (or to protect the heart in hyperkalaemia). Calcium given while phosphate is high risks metastatic calcification.
**Protect the kidneys**: avoid IV contrast and NSAIDs.

blocks.title: Dialysis
items: Consider **haemodialysis early** if standard measures fail, before renal injury becomes irreversible.
Indications: oliguria or uraemia, or persistent hyperkalaemia, hyperphosphataemia or a high calcium × phosphate product despite hydration.
TLS refractory to conventional therapy is a recognised indication for **urgent dialysis**. Involve the renal team early.

blocks.text: Rasburicase role differs between sources. Davidson's oncology chapter offers it **when other measures fail**, while its leukaemia section and Kumar & Clark give it **prophylactically to high-risk patients** and to treat established TLS. For exams: lower risk = allopurinol + fluids; high risk or established TLS = rasburicase + fluids (unless G6PD deficient).
Do **not alkalinise the urine** when phosphate is high: an alkaline urine increases calcium phosphate precipitation in the tubules.
Asymptomatic hyperuricaemia is usually left alone, but **in cancer patients about to be treated it is lowered** to prevent TLS.

cards.front: TLS biochemistry: which four serum values change, and in which direction?
cards.back: **High** potassium, phosphate and uric acid; **low** calcium ("PUKE Calcium").

cards.front: Why is calcium low in TLS?
cards.back: It is secondary: released phosphate binds and sequesters calcium.
Bulky, chemosensitive tumours: high-grade lymphoma (especially Burkitt), acute leukaemias and germ cell tumours.

cards.front: Name two non-cytotoxic drug triggers of TLS.
cards.back: Corticosteroids alone, and venetoclax at the start of treatment.

cards.front: Pre-treatment risk factors for TLS (besides tumour type)?
cards.back: Bulky disease, high LDH, high baseline uric acid and pre-existing renal impairment.

cards.front: How does TLS cause acute kidney injury?
cards.back: Urate (and calcium phosphate) crystals precipitate in the renal tubules, causing an obstructive crystal nephropathy.

cards.front: Which TLS abnormality is the main immediate danger?
cards.back: Hyperkalaemia, through cardiac arrhythmia and sudden death.

cards.front: Where does the uric acid in TLS come from?
cards.back: Breakdown of nucleic acids and purines released from the dying cells.

cards.front: How long should at-risk patients have biochemistry monitored after treatment?
cards.back: Regularly for 48–72 hours (Davidson); at least 72 hours in Burkitt lymphoma (Kumar & Clark).

cards.front: Prolonged QT in a patient with TLS points to which abnormality?
Single most important measure to prevent TLS?
cards.back: Aggressive IV hydration, started 24 h before treatment in high-risk patients.
Allopurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase (prevents urate formation). Rasburicase is urate oxidase (converts existing urate to soluble allantoin).
G6PD deficiency: it causes haemolytic anaemia.

cards.front: When should calcium be given in TLS?
cards.back: Only for symptomatic hypocalcaemia or hyperkalaemia; otherwise it risks metastatic calcification while phosphate is high.

cards.front: When is dialysis needed in TLS?
cards.back: When hydration and drugs fail: oliguria/uraemia, or persistent hyperkalaemia, hyperphosphataemia or high Ca × PO4 product. Start early, before damage is irreversible.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man with a large mediastinal mass from high-grade lymphoma receives his first cycle of chemotherapy. Thirty-six hours later he is nauseated and complains of muscle cramps. His urine output has fallen.
questions.leadIn: Which pattern of serum results is most likely?
options: Potassium high, phosphate low, urate high, calcium high
Potassium low, phosphate high, urate high, calcium low
Potassium high, phosphate high, urate high, calcium low
Potassium high, phosphate high, urate low, calcium high
Potassium low, phosphate low, urate low, calcium low
questions.explanation: Bulky high-grade lymphoma after the **first cycle** of chemotherapy is the classic setting for tumour lysis syndrome. Lysed cells release potassium, phosphate and purines (which become urate), so all three rise. Calcium **falls** because phosphate binds it: three highs, one low.
whyNot: Phosphate rises in TLS because it is released from cells, and calcium falls rather than rises.
Potassium is released from lysed cells, so it rises, not falls.
Urate rises from nucleic acid breakdown, and calcium falls, not rises.
Only calcium falls in TLS; the other three rise.

questions.stem: A medical student is reviewing the biochemistry of a patient who developed tumour lysis syndrome after induction chemotherapy for acute leukaemia.
questions.leadIn: Which abnormality arises because a substance released from the cells binds it, rather than from direct release?
questions.explanation: Hypocalcaemia is the only **secondary** abnormality in the tetrad: the large phosphate load released from the cells complexes with calcium and lowers its serum level.
whyNot: Potassium is an intracellular ion released directly when cells burst.
Phosphate is released directly from the cells; it is the cause of the low calcium, not a consequence of binding.
Urate comes from breakdown of released nucleic acids and purines, not from binding.
LDH is a pre-treatment marker of tumour bulk; it is not lowered or raised by another ion binding to it.

questions.stem: Five patients are about to start anticancer treatment this week.
questions.leadIn: Which patient is at the highest risk of tumour lysis syndrome?
options: A 63-year-old woman starting adjuvant chemotherapy after excision of a small breast cancer
A 15-year-old boy with Burkitt lymphoma, a bulky abdominal mass and a very high LDH
A 75-year-old man starting treatment for a slow-growing, localised prostate cancer
A 50-year-old woman having a basal cell carcinoma excised from her cheek
A 40-year-old man starting radioiodine after thyroidectomy for a small thyroid cancer
questions.explanation: TLS needs a **bulky, rapidly proliferating, chemosensitive** tumour. Burkitt lymphoma is the classic high-risk tumour, and a very high LDH reflects a large tumour burden.
whyNot: After excision the residual tumour burden is tiny, and TLS is very rare with solid tumours.
A slow-growing, localised tumour has neither the bulk nor the turnover needed.
Local excision of a small skin cancer does not release a large cell mass into the circulation.
A small residual thyroid cancer is low-burden and slow-growing.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old man with newly diagnosed acute lymphoblastic leukaemia and a very high white cell count is started on high-dose oral prednisolone alone while his cytogenetics are awaited. Two days later: K+ 6.3 mmol/L, phosphate high, urate high, corrected calcium low, creatinine rising. A repeat sample with prompt processing gives the same results.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely explanation?
options: Artefactual hyperkalaemia from release of potassium by leucocytes in the sample
Acute gout caused by the high white cell count
Tumour lysis syndrome triggered by the corticosteroid
Prerenal acute kidney injury from steroid-induced diuresis
Acute phosphate nephropathy from bowel preparation
questions.explanation: **Steroids alone** can kill enough lymphoblasts to cause TLS. The full pattern of high K+, phosphate and urate with low calcium and rising creatinine confirms a true lysis syndrome rather than a sampling artefact.
whyNot: Leucocytosis can falsely raise potassium, but a promptly processed repeat confirmed it, and artefact does not explain high phosphate, high urate, low calcium and rising creatinine.
Hyperuricaemia from cell turnover rarely causes gout, and gout does not explain the electrolyte pattern.
Prerenal AKI does not produce this combination of high phosphate, high urate and low calcium.
There is no history of oral phosphate bowel preparation.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman with acute myeloid leukaemia develops acute kidney injury 48 hours after her first dose of induction chemotherapy. Serum urate is markedly raised.
questions.leadIn: What is the main mechanism of her kidney injury?
options: Uric acid crystal precipitation within the renal tubules
questions.explanation: In TLS the filtered urate load is so high that **uric acid crystallises in the tubules**, causing an obstructive crystal nephropathy. Calcium phosphate deposition can add to it.
whyNot: Glomerular immune-complex disease is not how TLS damages the kidney.
Venous thrombosis is not the mechanism in TLS.
Calcium is low, not high, in TLS.
Papillary necrosis is not a feature of tumour lysis.

questions.stem: Two days after starting chemotherapy for bulky lymphoma, a 33-year-old man reports tingling around his mouth and painful hand cramps. Inflating a blood pressure cuff on his arm makes his wrist and fingers flex into spasm.
questions.leadIn: Which electrolyte disturbance directly produces these signs?
questions.explanation: Perioral paraesthesia, cramps and **Trousseau's sign** are features of neuromuscular irritability from **hypocalcaemia**. In TLS the calcium falls because of the phosphate load.
whyNot: Hyperkalaemia causes arrhythmias, not tetany.
Urate causes kidney injury, not tetany.
High phosphate is the upstream cause, but the signs come directly from the low calcium.
Hyponatraemia is not part of the TLS pattern and does not cause Trousseau's sign.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man with a bulky germ cell tumour is being monitored after his first cycle of chemotherapy because he is at high risk of tumour lysis syndrome.
questions.leadIn: Which result may be the earliest biochemical sign that TLS is developing?
options: Uric acid crystals in the urine
questions.explanation: Davidson notes that a **rising potassium** may be the earliest biochemical marker, so potassium is checked closely for 48–72 hours after treatment.
whyNot: Calcium falls only after phosphate has risen, so it is a later change.
Creatinine rises once crystal nephropathy has developed, which is later.
LDH is used before treatment to estimate tumour bulk, not as the earliest marker of lysis.
Crystalluria reflects established urate nephropathy rather than the earliest change.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman with newly diagnosed high-grade lymphoma is being worked up before chemotherapy. The team wants a blood test that reflects tumour bulk and helps estimate her TLS risk.
questions.leadIn: Which test is most useful for this purpose?
questions.explanation: Pre-treatment **LDH** correlates with tumour bulk and flags increased TLS risk. It is also used in lymphoma staging. A baseline uric acid is useful too.
whyNot: ALP reflects bone or liver involvement, not overall tumour bulk for TLS risk.
CRP is a non-specific inflammatory marker and does not estimate TLS risk.
Ferritin is not used to assess tumour bulk or TLS risk.
Troponin assesses myocardial injury, not tumour burden.

questions.stem: A 21-year-old woman with T-lymphoblastic leukaemia and a high white cell count is due to start induction chemotherapy tomorrow.
questions.leadIn: Which is the single most important measure to prevent tumour lysis syndrome?
options: Aggressive IV hydration started before treatment
questions.explanation: **Hydration** dilutes the released ions and increases renal blood flow and filtration, so potassium, phosphate and urate are excreted. In high-risk patients it starts 24 hours before treatment.
whyNot: Calcium is given only for symptomatic hypocalcaemia or hyperkalaemia, not as prophylaxis.
Restricting fluid would reduce urine flow and encourage crystal deposition.
Dialysis is reserved for failure of standard measures, not routine prevention.
Alkalinisation is avoided when phosphate is high because it promotes calcium phosphate precipitation.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man with high-risk lymphoma is about to start chemotherapy. His urate is moderately raised. A screening test shows he has G6PD deficiency.
questions.leadIn: Which urate-lowering plan is most appropriate?
options: Fluid restriction with a loop diuretic
questions.explanation: Rasburicase is **contraindicated in G6PD deficiency** because it causes haemolysis. The safe option is **allopurinol**, which blocks urate formation, combined with vigorous hydration.
whyNot: Rasburicase can cause haemolytic anaemia in G6PD deficiency.
Alkalinisation does not lower urate production and risks calcium phosphate precipitation.
Fluid restriction lowers urine flow, the opposite of what is needed.
Phosphate supplements worsen hyperphosphataemia.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man with a testicular germ cell tumour and bulky retroperitoneal nodes starts chemotherapy. On day 2: K+ 6.4 mmol/L, phosphate high, corrected calcium low, urate high, creatinine double baseline. Creatine kinase is normal and he has had no bowel preparation.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Germ cell tumours are bulky and chemosensitive, and the **three highs, one low** pattern after the first cycle is diagnostic of TLS. A normal CK argues against muscle breakdown.
whyNot: Rhabdomyolysis also shifts potassium out of cells, but the CK is normal.
His calcium is low, not high.
Phosphate nephropathy follows oral phosphate bowel preparation, which he has not had.
No contrast is mentioned, and contrast does not cause hyperuricaemia or hypocalcaemia.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man develops hyperkalaemia 24 hours after chemotherapy for acute leukaemia. A repeat sample confirms it.
questions.leadIn: What is the main mechanism of his hyperkalaemia?
options: Shift of potassium from lysed cells into the plasma
questions.explanation: In TLS the hyperkalaemia is a **redistribution** problem: intracellular K+ floods into plasma when cells burst, the same mechanism as rhabdomyolysis and severe haemolysis. Reduced excretion from AKI can add to it.
whyNot: There is no reason for aldosterone deficiency here.
Diet does not explain an abrupt rise after chemotherapy.
The repeat sample confirmed the result, so this is not artefactual.
Alkalosis moves potassium into cells, lowering it.

questions.stem: On the second day of chemotherapy for Burkitt lymphoma, a 17-year-old boy has a brief generalised seizure. His ECG shows a prolonged QT interval with normal T waves.
questions.leadIn: Which substance released from the tumour cells is ultimately responsible for his QT prolongation?
questions.explanation: Two steps: a prolonged QT with seizures points to **hypocalcaemia**, and in TLS hypocalcaemia is caused by the **phosphate** load, which binds calcium.
whyNot: Potassium excess causes peaked T waves and broad QRS, not a long QT.
Urate causes kidney injury, not QT prolongation.
LDH is a marker of tumour bulk with no electrical effect.
Purines become urate, which does not lower calcium.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with acute leukaemia develops acute kidney injury two days after induction chemotherapy. The team suspects urate nephropathy.
questions.leadIn: Which investigations best support this cause?
options: Urine microscopy for crystals and serum urate
CT angiography of the renal arteries
questions.explanation: For suspected urate crystal nephropathy after tumour lysis, look for **uric acid crystals on urine microscopy** and a raised **serum urate**.
whyNot: Complement levels help with cholesterol emboli or thrombotic microangiopathy, not urate nephropathy.
Anti-GBM antibodies look for anti-GBM disease.
Urine oxalate investigates oxalate nephropathy, not urate.
CT angiography looks for vascular causes of AKI.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old woman develops AKI on day 3 of chemotherapy for high-grade lymphoma. The team wants a urine test that points specifically to acute uric acid nephropathy.
questions.leadIn: Which urine finding best supports this diagnosis?
options: Fractional sodium excretion below 1% with a bland sediment
Dysmorphic red cells and red cell casts
Urine uric acid to creatinine ratio above 1
questions.explanation: In acute uric acid nephropathy the urine **urate:creatinine ratio is above 1**, and uric acid crystals may be seen in the sediment.
whyNot: A low FENa with bland urine suggests prerenal AKI.
Dysmorphic red cells and casts suggest glomerulonephritis.
Nephrotic-range proteinuria points to glomerular disease.
Oxalate crystals point to oxalate nephropathy, not urate.

questions.stem: A patient with tumour lysis syndrome has a serum K+ of 6.9 mmol/L. His ECG shows tall peaked T waves and a widening QRS.
questions.leadIn: Which treatment most rapidly protects his heart?
options: IV sodium bicarbonate to alkalinise the urine
questions.explanation: Hyperkalaemia is the immediate threat in TLS. **IV calcium gluconate stabilises the myocardium**; insulin with dextrose then shifts K+ into cells. Calcium is appropriate here despite the high phosphate because hyperkalaemia is present.
whyNot: Rasburicase lowers urate; it does nothing for potassium.
Binders treat phosphate, not potassium.
Allopurinol only prevents new urate formation; it does nothing for potassium.
Urinary alkalinisation is avoided with high phosphate and does not protect the heart.

questions.stem: On day 2 of treatment for acute leukaemia, a 35-year-old woman has a low corrected calcium and a very high phosphate. She has no paraesthesia, cramps or tetany. K+ is 5.2 mmol/L and the ECG is normal.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate approach to her calcium?
options: Give IV calcium gluconate to normalise the calcium
Treat the phosphate (IV saline, phosphate binder) and withhold calcium while she is asymptomatic
Give oral phosphate to rebalance the calcium-phosphate product
Alkalinise the urine with sodium bicarbonate
questions.explanation: Calcium is reserved for **symptomatic** hypocalcaemia or hyperkalaemia, because adding calcium to a high phosphate risks **metastatic calcification**. Lowering phosphate corrects the cause.
whyNot: Routine IV calcium with high phosphate risks calcium phosphate deposition.
Unwarranted vitamin D aggravates hyperphosphataemia.
Extra phosphate would worsen both the hyperphosphataemia and the hypocalcaemia.
Alkalinisation with high phosphate increases calcium phosphate precipitation.

questions.stem: A man with TLS has had vigorous IV fluids, diuretics and rasburicase for 24 hours. He has passed 150 mL of urine in 12 hours, K+ remains 7.0 mmol/L, and phosphate keeps rising.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate next step?
questions.explanation: Oliguria with **refractory hyperkalaemia and rising phosphate** despite standard therapy is an indication for **early haemodialysis**, before kidney injury becomes irreversible.
whyNot: Allopurinol only prevents new urate formation and will not fix the potassium.
Urate is not the problem now; potassium and phosphate are.
Fluid restriction does not treat refractory hyperkalaemia.
Alkalinisation is avoided with high phosphate.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old boy has newly diagnosed Burkitt lymphoma with a large abdominal mass. Before treatment: LDH very high, urate raised, creatinine mildly raised. G6PD screen is normal. Chemotherapy is planned within 24 hours.
questions.leadIn: Which prophylactic plan is most appropriate?
options: No prophylaxis; check electrolytes once after the first cycle
Encourage oral fluids and start allopurinol after chemotherapy
IV hydration started before treatment plus rasburicase
Fluid restriction to protect the impaired kidneys
questions.explanation:
**Step 1 – grade the risk.** Burkitt lymphoma, a bulky mass, high LDH, raised baseline urate and renal impairment all put him at **high risk**.
**Step 2 – hydrate.** High-risk patients start vigorous IV fluids **before** treatment (Davidson: 24 h ahead) to keep urine output high.
**Step 3 – choose the urate drug.** Urate is already high, so a drug that only blocks new production is not enough. **Rasburicase** breaks down existing urate, and his normal G6PD makes it safe.
**Step 4 – monitor** K+ and phosphate very frequently for at least 72 hours.
whyNot: High-risk patients need prophylaxis and frequent monitoring, not a single check.
Oral fluids are inadequate, and prophylaxis must start before chemotherapy, not after.
Dialysis is for failure of standard measures, not prevention.
Restricting fluid reduces urine flow and promotes crystal nephropathy.

questions.stem: Thirty hours after starting chemotherapy for AML, a 58-year-old woman feels weak. Results: K+ 6.8 mmol/L, phosphate 2.6 mmol/L, corrected calcium 1.9 mmol/L, urate markedly raised, creatinine 190 µmol/L. She has no tetany.
questions.leadIn: Which abnormality poses the most immediate threat to her life?
questions.explanation:
**Step 1 – recognise TLS:** three highs (K+, phosphate, urate) and one low (calcium) after induction for a leukaemia.
**Step 2 – rank the dangers.** Urate and phosphate harm the kidneys over hours to days. Her hypocalcaemia is asymptomatic. **Potassium** can cause a fatal arrhythmia at any moment.
**Step 3 – act:** ECG, IV calcium gluconate if ECG changes, insulin-dextrose, and continued hydration.
whyNot: Urate drives kidney injury, which is serious but slower.
Phosphate matters mainly through calcium binding and tubular deposition, not sudden death.
Her low calcium is asymptomatic and is treated only if symptoms develop.
The creatinine reflects AKI, which is dangerous mainly because it impairs potassium excretion.

questions.stem: A 39-year-old man with bulky high-grade lymphoma has just finished his first day of chemotherapy. He is at high risk of TLS.
questions.leadIn: Which monitoring plan is most appropriate?
options: Serum K+, phosphate, calcium, urate and creatinine regularly for 48–72 hours
Serum LDH daily for two weeks
Serum calcium only, until the next cycle
questions.explanation:
**Step 1 – timing:** TLS develops in the first days after treatment, so watch closely for **48–72 hours** (at least 72 h in Burkitt).
**Step 2 – what to measure:** each element of the tetrad (K+, phosphate, calcium, urate) plus **renal function**, because AKI both results from and worsens TLS.
**Step 3 – the earliest clue** is often a rising potassium.
whyNot: A single urate misses the potassium rise, which is often the earliest and most dangerous change.
The blood count does not detect the metabolic changes of TLS.
LDH is a pre-treatment marker of bulk, not a monitoring test for lysis.
Calcium alone misses hyperkalaemia and renal failure.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with chronic lymphocytic leukaemia and bulky nodes is starting venetoclax.
questions.leadIn: Which complication requires particularly close laboratory surveillance as this drug is started?
questions.explanation: **Venetoclax** is specifically associated with TLS at initiation, so electrolytes and renal function are monitored closely.
whyNot: Cardiotoxicity is linked with other agents and is not the early laboratory concern here.
Infertility is a late effect and not monitored with blood chemistry at the start.
Neurotoxicity is not the specific early risk of this drug.
Second cancers are a long-term risk, not an early laboratory emergency.

questions.stem: A patient with early TLS and a rising phosphate is constipated on day 2 of treatment. Several remedies are suggested.
questions.leadIn: Which would most aggravate his hyperphosphataemia?
questions.explanation: Hyperphosphataemia in TLS comes from cellular release and is **made worse by phosphate-containing preparations** (and unwarranted vitamin D).
whyNot: Saline promotes phosphate excretion.
Binders lower phosphate absorption.
Dialysis removes phosphate.
Rasburicase acts on urate and does not add phosphate.

questions.stem: A pharmacology tutor asks how rasburicase lowers serum urate in tumour lysis syndrome.
questions.leadIn: What is its mechanism of action?
options: Oxidises uric acid to soluble allantoin
Binds uric acid in the gut
questions.explanation: Rasburicase is a **recombinant urate oxidase**: it converts existing uric acid to **allantoin**, which is far more soluble. Allopurinol, by contrast, inhibits xanthine oxidase.
whyNot: That is allopurinol's mechanism.
Rasburicase is an enzyme, not a uricosuric.
It is given IV and acts in the circulation, not in the gut.
It degrades urate already formed; it does not block purine synthesis.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old with high-risk lymphoma received rasburicase yesterday. Today his serum urate is reported as undetectable. K+ is 5.8 mmol/L and creatinine is unchanged.
questions.leadIn: What is the best interpretation?
options: Laboratory error; repeat the urate before acting
TLS has resolved, so monitoring can stop
An expected drug effect; continue monitoring electrolytes and renal function
Haemolysed sample causing falsely low urate
questions.explanation: Rasburicase oxidises urate so effectively that levels can become **undetectable**. That does not mean the lysis has stopped: his potassium is still raised, so keep monitoring K+, phosphate, calcium and creatinine.
whyNot: An undetectable urate after rasburicase is expected, not an error.
Potassium is still high; TLS has not resolved.
Haemolysis would cause anaemia; it does not explain the undetectable urate.
In-vitro haemolysis raises potassium; it does not make urate vanish.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man starting chemotherapy for acute leukaemia develops a very high serum urate.
questions.leadIn: What is the main clinical risk of this hyperuricaemia?
questions.explanation: Hyperuricaemia from increased purine turnover during chemotherapy **seldom causes gout**; the danger is urate crystal deposition in the tubules causing **acute kidney injury**.
whyNot: Gout is seldom triggered by treatment-related hyperuricaemia.
Tophi take years of hyperuricaemia to form.
Pseudogout is due to calcium pyrophosphate, not urate.
The injury in TLS is acute, not chronic.

questions.stem: A woman with established TLS and AKI complains of bone pain on day 3 of chemotherapy. The team considers analgesia.
questions.leadIn: Which drug should be avoided?
questions.explanation: In TLS, **NSAIDs and IV contrast** are avoided because they add further insult to kidneys already injured by crystal nephropathy.
whyNot: Paracetamol is not singled out as harmful to the kidney here.
Saline is part of TLS treatment.
Allopurinol is used to prevent further urate formation.
Insulin-dextrose is a treatment for hyperkalaemia.

questions.theme: Tumour lysis syndrome: choosing the intervention
questions.leadIn: Pick the single best next intervention for each patient below. An option can be chosen for one patient, several patients, or none.

items.stem: A 70-year-old man with lymphoma, a low TLS risk and a normal baseline urate is starting chemotherapy. IV fluids are already running. The team wants an oral drug to stop new uric acid from being made.
items.explanation: Allopurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase and prevents urate formation. With fluids, it is the standard prophylaxis for lower-risk patients.

items.stem: On day 1 after induction for ALL, a 22-year-old has K+ 7.1 mmol/L. The ECG shows absent P waves and a broad QRS.
items.explanation: With ECG changes of hyperkalaemia, the first priority is myocardial protection with IV calcium gluconate, followed by insulin-dextrose.

items.stem: Despite 36 hours of IV fluids, diuretics and a urate-lowering drug, a 47-year-old with TLS is oliguric, K+ stays above 6.5 mmol/L and the calcium × phosphate product keeps climbing.
items.explanation: Persistent hyperkalaemia and hyperphosphataemia with falling urine output despite standard measures needs early dialysis.

items.stem: A 14-year-old with Burkitt lymphoma has a markedly raised urate and bulky disease before treatment. G6PD activity is normal and IV fluids have been started. The team wants to lower the urate that is already present.
items.explanation: Two steps: urate already present needs an enzyme that breaks it down, not one that blocks new production; with normal G6PD, rasburicase is safe and is the drug of choice in high-risk patients.

questions.stem: A cancer centre audits which patients develop tumour lysis syndrome during their first course of treatment.
questions.leadIn: Which tumour is most classically associated with TLS?
questions.explanation: TLS is most common when treating **high-grade lymphomas (especially Burkitt)** and acute leukaemias: fast-growing, bulky, chemosensitive tumours.
whyNot: A localised, slow-growing solid tumour has too little turnover.
Early breast cancer has a small burden; TLS is very rare with solid tumours.
A slow-growing solid tumour with low burden.
A small, locally invasive skin cancer that is not treated with intensive chemotherapy.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman with bulky acute lymphoblastic leukaemia is judged to be at high risk of tumour lysis syndrome. Induction chemotherapy is planned.
questions.leadIn: When should IV hydration begin?
options: Only once serum potassium starts to rise
Only after rasburicase has been given
After the full course is completed
questions.explanation: Davidson advises starting hydration **24 hours before treatment** in high-risk patients and maintaining a good urine output throughout.
whyNot: Waiting for hyperkalaemia means prevention has already failed.
TLS occurs in the first 48–72 hours, so this is too late.
Hydration is the cornerstone and is not delayed for drug therapy.
Hydration is needed during treatment, when lysis happens.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man develops AKI after the first dose of chemotherapy for acute leukaemia. Urine microscopy shows crystals.
questions.leadIn: Which type of crystal is most likely?
questions.explanation: **Uric acid crystals** form from tumour lysis, typically as a **first-dose effect** of chemotherapy in haematological malignancy.
whyNot: Oxalate crystals follow fat malabsorption or ethylene glycol.
Cystine crystals reflect an inherited tubular disorder, not chemotherapy.
Sulphonamide crystals follow sulphonamide drugs.
Cholesterol emboli are not urinary crystals of tumour lysis.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old woman develops tumour lysis syndrome after chemotherapy for high-grade lymphoma.
questions.leadIn: Which serum value is expected to be low?
questions.explanation: Remember **PUKE Calcium**: phosphate, urate and K+ are elevated; **calcium is low** because phosphate binds it.
whyNot: Potassium is released from cells and rises.
Phosphate is released from cells and rises.
Urate rises from nucleic acid breakdown.
Creatinine rises if AKI develops.

questions.stem: A 57-year-old man with TLS has a markedly raised serum phosphate and is asymptomatic. He is passing urine and his potassium is controlled.
questions.leadIn: Which measure does Davidson recommend to promote phosphate excretion?
questions.explanation: Davidson treats hyperphosphataemia from tumour lysis with **IV normal saline**, which increases phosphate excretion. Phosphate binders are another option.
whyNot: Vitamin D increases phosphate absorption and aggravates the problem.
Calcium is given only for symptomatic hypocalcaemia or hyperkalaemia; with high phosphate it risks metastatic calcification.
Alkalinisation increases calcium phosphate precipitation when phosphate is high.
Phosphate-containing preparations worsen hyperphosphataemia.
